quote: Tracing back the chain of causality, step by step, I discover that my belief that I’m wearing socks is fully explained by the fact that I’m wearing socks. This is right and proper, as you cannot gain information about something without interacting with it.
content: The rule being applied is the causal theory of knowledge (Goldman (1967)): a belief is justified when its causal history runs through the fact it is about. The rule has a famous failure mode, and the failure mode covers the book’s own commitments. Beliefs about numbers, sets, logical truths, and probabilities have no causal history running through their objects, because those objects do not cause anything (Benacerraf (1973)); by the sock test they are “explained away.” The same argument, run on evaluative beliefs, is Street’s Darwinian dilemma (Street (2006)): the causal history of a moral belief runs through selection, not through moral facts, so the realist must say the beliefs are mirages. This book asserts that “reality is math” and that probability theory is a law; the causal chain behind those beliefs runs through textbooks and intuitions, not through mathematical objects, and the essay’s method, applied consistently, classifies its own foundations with the lake in the desert. Goldman himself abandoned the causal theory for reliabilism partly for this reason. The sock example works because socks are the easy case.

quote: Where’s the free-will-sensor in your brain, and how does it detect the presence or absence of free will? How does the sensor interact with the sensed event, and what are the mechanical details of the interaction?
content: The question had been answered, at the level of detail the essay asks for, nine years earlier. Wegner and Wheatley’s theory of apparent mental causation (Wegner & Wheatley (1999); Wegner, The Illusion of Conscious Will, 2002) specifies the “sensor”: the experience of willing an act arises when a thought about the act precedes it, is consistent with it, and no other cause is salient, and each of the three conditions was manipulated experimentally to produce or abolish the feeling (the “I Spy” study, in which a confederate’s prompting produced a sense of authorship over a cursor movement the participant did not make). Whether this shows free will to be an illusion is exactly what the essay says one cannot settle by tracing: the sensor detects priority, consistency and exclusivity, and a compatibilist (Dennett, Elbow Room, 1984, a book with no DOI) says those are the very properties that constitute acting freely, so the sensor is detecting something real. The rhetorical question assumes that a sensor for a real property would look like a retina for photons; the free-will sensor looks like a sensor for a relation between one’s own states, which is what compatibilist free will is. The trace does not decide between the two readings, and the essay’s claim that it is “guaranteed to have an answer” is true only of the trace, not of the question.

quote: On the other hand, if I see a mirage of a lake in a desert, the correct causal explanation of my vision does not involve the fact of any actual lake in the desert. In this case, my belief in the lake is not just explained, but explained away.
content: The two cases are presented as a dichotomy and they are the ends of a continuum on which almost every interesting belief sits in the middle. The mirage is caused by real skylight refracted by a real temperature gradient plus a visual system whose prior interprets a bright horizontal region as water; the socks are seen by the same system resolving an ambiguous retinal image with the same kind of prior (perception as unconscious inference, Helmholtz 1867, and the modern predictive-processing literature). In both cases the belief is explained by an external fact and by the machinery; what differs is whether the external fact is the one the belief names. For perceptual beliefs the difference is usually clear. For the beliefs the essay wants to apply the method to (free will, consciousness, the direction of time, “why does reality exist”), the whole dispute is over what the belief names, and the tracing exercise returns “an algorithm plus some external facts” for every one of them, which each side then reads its own way. The method is guaranteed to produce a causal story; it is not guaranteed to produce a verdict, and the essay slides from the first guarantee to the second.
